week.t: Quanta: 41% of the interstellar gas in our galactic neighbourhood is in a state a 1969 theory said should barely exist
NASA opens Dragonfly’s passenger list: names fly to Titan, deadline 15 Jan 2027
Science: Manx shearwaters get jet lag and drift up to 15° off their heading
MSS: inter-monsoon conditions setting in; haze expected to improve
PIB backgrounder: India’s NGLV designed for 30 tonnes to low Earth orbit
A*STAR, NRP, NTU and Micron launch Singapore’s first Embodied AI Challenge

tiles.cap: Your name can fly to Titan on NASA’s Dragonfly. The passenger list closes 15 January
tiles.nums: the year Dragonfly arrives at Saturn’s moon Titan, after a launch scheduled for 2028
tiles.p1: NASA is inviting the public to send their names aboard Dragonfly, a rotorcraft, and be part of the first science mission to fly and explore the surface of another world. The passenger list is open until 11:59 pm US Eastern time on 15 January 2027. Scheduled to launch in 2028, Dragonfly will travel to Titan, a world with a thick atmosphere, rivers and lakes of liquid methane, sweeping dunes and a landscape rich in organic material.
tiles.p2: Why it matters to you: NASA’s sign-up is a web form called “Send Your Name to Titan”, and it issues a personalised digital boarding pass. The deadline in Singapore time is 12:59 pm on Saturday 16 January.
deep: A rotorcraft on another moon

After arriving in 2034, Dragonfly will fly to different locations on the moon, exploring Titan’s diverse environments and searching for clues about prebiotic chemistry, the chemistry that came before biology, to help scientists better understand the ingredients and conditions for life.
Flying, not driving

NASA describes Titan as a remarkable world with a thick atmosphere, rivers and lakes of liquid methane, sweeping dunes and a landscape rich in organic material. Dragonfly will fly to different locations on the moon; NASA calls it the first science mission to fly and explore the surface of another world.
Who runs it

Dragonfly is the fourth mission in NASA’s New Frontiers Program, managed by NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, for the agency’s Science Mission Directorate. Elizabeth Turtle of APL, the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, is the principal investigator.
The arithmetic of waiting
Sign up by January 2027, launch in 2028, arrive in 2034: your name spends about six years in flight. Add eight to your age now, and that is how old you will be when it lands.

tiles.cap: Nobody knocks on the ISS hatch at Halloween, so astronauts build costumes from cargo boxes
tiles.nums: years of continuous human presence aboard the space station, and a costume album to match
tiles.p1: NASA’s Johnson Space Center posted its Halloween album from orbit on Thursday 29 October. Although no ghouls, goblins or trick-or-treaters come knocking at the International Space Station’s front hatch, crews still dress up, in costumes often designed from materials available aboard the station. In 2022, Koichi Wakata of JAXA and NASA astronauts Frank Rubio, Nicole Mann and Josh Cassada dressed as video game and cartoon characters, using stowage containers in their costumes and holding improvised trick-or-treat bags.
tiles.p2: Why now: Halloween was Saturday. The photo on this tile is from Expedition 57, when Commander Alexander Gerst of ESA dressed as Darth Vader.
deep: Elvis, Vader and a mad scientist

Flight Engineer Sergei Prokopyev of Roscosmos dressed as Elvis Presley, Commander Alexander Gerst of ESA as Darth Vader, and Flight Engineer Serena Auñón-Chancellor of NASA as a mad scientist, posing inside the Kibo Japanese Experiment Module during Expedition 57.
Superman at last
ESA astronaut Luca Parmitano finally got his wish to fly like Superman aboard the station during Expedition 37. In orbit, the flying part needs no special effects.
Made from what is up there

Costumes are often designed from materials available aboard the space station. In 2022 the Expedition 68 crew used stowage containers in their outfits; in 2023 Jasmin Moghbeli, Satoshi Furukawa, Loral O’Hara and Andreas Mogensen celebrated together.
Back to work

NASA’s station blog on Friday 30 October: Anil Menon and Joshua Kutryk will install the eighth and final roll-out solar array on Thursday 5 November, raising the station’s power generating capacity from 160 kilowatts to about 215 kilowatts.
tiles.src: NASA Johnson, 29 Oct 2026 (John Uri) · NASA Space Station blog, 30 Oct 2026 (Mark A. Garcia)

tiles.cap: “Empty” space holds about 130 hydrogen atoms per litre. Two-fifths of it should not exist
tiles.nums: of the interstellar gas in our galactic neighbourhood sits in an “unstable” state that a 1969 theory said should barely exist
tiles.p1: You might imagine space to be empty. But the seeming void between the stars contains a barely perceptible fog of hydrogen and other neutral atoms: New Horizons found around 130 hydrogen atoms per litre of space. A 1969 model by George Field, Donald Goldsmith and Harm Habing said this gas should sit in one of two states, cold at about 100 kelvins (minus 173 degrees Celsius) or warm near 8,000 kelvins, with almost nothing in between.
tiles.p2: Why it is a good story: the person who found the in-between gas was an undergraduate, Jonathan Shelest at the Technion in Haifa, and his first thought was that he had made a mistake.
deep: The map

Gaia observed almost 2 billion stars from different angles as Earth moved around the Sun. In 2024 a separate team used such tools to build a continuous three-dimensional map of the density of interstellar dust inside a sphere more than 4,000 light-years wide around our Sun. Shelest and his professor Shmuel Bialy used that kind of map to work out the state of the gas.
The forbidden zone

Shelest found that 27% of the ISM in our galactic neighbourhood was cold, 32% was warm, and the remaining 41% sat squarely in the forbidden zone as unstable medium. “I thought I was wrong,” he said. Tested on a different, lower-resolution dust map, the unstable fraction shifted by only about 5%.
Blankets around clouds

Instead of vanishing, the unstable gas formed massive, coherent blankets that wrapped around the cold clouds completely. “All that midrange medium, neither hot nor cold, implies that the older theory is incomplete,” said Adam Ginsburg of the University of Florida.
Where it stands
The paper was posted in July 2026 and is undergoing peer review. On the day it went up, Shelest’s inbox filled with messages from excited astronomers and requests to collaborate.

tiles.cap: Seabirds get jet lag. Fly east or west fast enough and they veer up to 15° off their line
tiles.nums: breeding Manx shearwaters fitted with miniature GPS trackers over 20 years by Tim Guilford and colleagues at Oxford
tiles.p1: Jet lag isn’t just for travellers hurtling across time zones. Manx shearwaters fly fast enough to experience it, researchers reported on Thursday 29 October in Science. Decades of tracking data from foraging flights revealed that rapid east-west journeys can throw the seabirds’ internal clocks out of sync with local time, causing them to misjudge the Sun’s position and veer slightly off their heading.
tiles.p2: Connects to: your own body clock on a flight to London does the same thing. The difference is that you do not steer by the Sun.
deep: A compass that needs a watch

Scientists have long predicted that the mismatch between a bird’s internal clock and local time could confound its sun-based compass, but testing the idea in the wild “has seemed impossible until now,” says Tim Guilford, a biologist at the University of Oxford.
20 years of trackers

Over 20 years, Guilford and colleagues equipped 1,045 breeding Manx shearwaters with miniature GPS trackers. The trackers logged thousands of trips from United Kingdom breeding colonies to feeding grounds up to 1,000 kilometres away; the team isolated 1,837 continuous homeward flights.
15 degrees
The birds veered as expected, by as much as 15 degrees from their intended direction. The birds seem to process and integrate multiple navigational cues without relying blindly on any one of them.
An Indian angle
This navigational tug-of-war excites Sangeeta Rani, a chronobiologist at the University of Lucknow in India.
tiles.src: Science News, 29 Oct 2026 (Anirban Mukhopadhyay) · Science, 29 Oct 2026

tiles.cap: The haze is set to ease: inter-monsoon winds arrive, with thundery afternoons on most days
tiles.nums: the hottest reading of 16 to 28 October, at Woodlands on 23 October; the next fortnight should run 33 to 35 °C
tiles.p1: With the weakening of the Southwest Monsoon, inter-monsoon conditions have been progressively setting in over Singapore and the surrounding region, the Meteorological Service Singapore said on Thursday 29 October. The inter-monsoon period is characterised by light and variable winds, as well as increased showers and higher lightning activity. Together with wetter conditions over Singapore and the nearby areas, the smoke haze situation is expected to improve.
tiles.p2: Why here: between 16 and 28 October, air quality reached “Unhealthy” levels for seven days and “Very Unhealthy” levels for three. Watch the air-quality readings over the next two weeks and see whether the forecast holds.
deep: What changed in the wind

With winds blowing mostly from the southeast or southwest, smoke haze was transported to Singapore. The inter-monsoon period brings light and variable winds, more showers and more lightning, and that is what is expected to improve the haze.
The fortnight ahead

In the first fortnight of November 2026, moderate to heavy thundery showers are expected over parts of the island in the afternoon on most days. Total rainfall is forecast to be slightly above its long-term average over most parts of the island; daily maximum temperatures between 33 and 35 degrees Celsius on most days, slightly above 35 on a few days.
Late October’s extremes

On 21 October, heavy thundery showers fell over western Singapore, with the fortnight’s highest daily total, 81.0 mm, at Tuas South. The highest daily maximum temperature, 36.1 degrees Celsius, was recorded at Woodlands on 23 October. Tanjong Katong had rainfall 72 per cent below average; Punggol 24 per cent above.
November normally
The climate-station averages for November, 1991 to 2020: daily maximum 31.2 °C, daily minimum 24.6 °C, 252.3 mm of rain over 19 rain days. This fortnight’s forecast is slightly wetter than that.
tiles.src: NEA / Meteorological Service Singapore advisory, 29 Oct 2026

tiles.cap: Teach a robot to open a chip-factory chamber and put it back together: S$88,000 in prizes
tiles.nums: top prize in Singapore’s first national Embodied AI Challenge; onsite finals at RoboSG! on 20 March 2027
tiles.p1: The National Robotics Programme, A*STAR, PINE Lab@NTU and Micron Technology have launched the Singapore Embodied AI Challenge for Manufacturing, Singapore’s first national-level competition dedicated to advancing embodied AI and robotics through real-world industry challenges. It was launched at ITAP on 21 October; the press release followed on Monday 26 October. Participants develop embodied AI solutions using a robotic embodiment platform to perform precise industrial manipulation tasks within a 3D mock-up chamber developed by Micron.
tiles.p2: Why here: it is open to teams worldwide, teams may comprise one to five members, and the online simulation phase is currently underway until 31 December 2026.
deep: The tasks

Teams will programme robots to execute tasks such as opening the chamber, removing and reinstalling components, conducting inspections, cleaning surfaces, and completing reassembly procedures. Teams will be ranked based on the number of operational steps they successfully complete.
How it runs

The competition begins with an online simulation phase, underway until 31 December 2026, which is also when registration closes. The highest-scoring teams advance to the onsite finals at RoboSG! 2027 on 20 March 2027, with shortlisted overseas teams eligible for travel subsidies.
Who supplies what

Infineon Technologies will contribute sensor technologies, while Galbot will provide a robotic platform, developer toolkit, robot hardware, and support for real-world data collection. Lightwheel and the National Supercomputing Centre (NSCC) Singapore support the competition infrastructure: simulation, benchmarking, evaluation and AI cloud computing.
The phrase to know

“Embodied AI represents the next frontier in robotics, bridging the gap between digital intelligence and physical execution,” says Prof Ziwei Wang, Director of PINE Lab@NTU. The total prize pool is S$88,000.

tiles.cap: India’s next rocket is designed to lift 30 tonnes to orbit, triple what LVM3 can carry
tiles.nums: how long ISRO’s home-built 300 mN plasma thruster ran in a life test completed on 27 March 2025
tiles.p1: In September 2024, the Union Cabinet approved the development of the Next Generation Launch Vehicle (NGLV). Designed for a maximum capacity of 30 tonnes to low Earth orbit, the NGLV triples India’s current launch payload capability compared with the 10-tonne limit of the LVM3. The figures come from a PIB backgrounder drawing on Department of Space material, released on Wednesday 28 October, during the ESTIC 2026 conclave in New Delhi.
tiles.p2: Why it matters to you: the same note says India now looks ahead to the planned Bharatiya Antariksh Station, its own space station, with Gaganyaan advancing India’s human spaceflight goals.
deep: From Thumba to 30 tonnes

India’s space journey began with a sounding rocket launched from Thumba, Kerala, on 21 November 1963. ISRO was formed on 15 August 1969, superseding INCOSPAR, and was brought under the Department of Space in 1972.
An electric engine

On 27 March 2025, ISRO completed a 1,000-hour life test of its indigenous 300 mN stationary plasma thruster. 300 millinewtons is about the weight of a 30-gram object, and 1,000 hours is nearly six weeks of continuous running: electric thrusters push gently for a long time.
Technology out the door

NewSpace India Limited (NSIL) has signed 118 Technology Transfer Agreements to transfer 83 technologies developed by ISRO to Indian industry. Cumulative investment in Indian space start-ups reached approximately US$618.5 million as of 31 March 2026.
The target

As per the Department of Space, India’s space economy is targeted to reach US$44 billion by 2033. ISRO is also collaborating with the Department of Atomic Energy on RHU and RTG requirements, radioisotope heater units and thermoelectric generators, for possible future Chandrayaan and Mars missions.
tiles.src: PIB backgrounder “India’s New-Age Space Technologies”, 28 Oct 2026 (PIB Research; sources include the Department of Space)

tiles.cap: Flatten a straw, snip two lips, blow: a buzzing oboe. Snip it shorter and the note climbs
tiles.nums: the speed of every sound wave in air, high note or low, according to the Exploratorium
tiles.p1: Sound is a branch of mechanics, Feynman says, and so it is to be understood in terms of Newton’s laws: move something in the air and the air is compressed, a change of pressure is produced which pushes on additional air, and the disturbance travels. The Exploratorium’s Straw Oboe lets you hear the whole chain. Flatten one end of a plastic straw between your teeth, cut equal pieces from each side of the flattened end so the straw has two “lips”, seal your lips around it and blow, adjusting how hard you bite and blow until the straw sings.
tiles.p2: Test it: snip the straw shorter and shorter with scissors. In a shorter straw the standing wave inside is shorter too, so the pitch is higher; in a longer straw the note is lower.
deep: The reed

The bevelled lips act as a reed. When you blow, there is high pressure in your mouth; as air rushes through the straw, the pressure in the straw drops; the high pressure outside pushes the sides of the reed inward, closing off the flow; the pressure then builds inside and pops the reed open again.
Resonance

The sound is an example of resonance: when you vibrate something at its natural frequency, the vibrations build and grow more and more extreme. The straw resonates when the sound waves bouncing back and forth inside make a standing wave, and the exact note depends on the length of the straw.
Newton was wrong, Laplace was right

Newton argued that heat was conducted between regions so rapidly that the temperature could not rise or fall. Feynman: “This argument gives the isothermal speed of sound, and it is wrong.” Laplace put forward the opposite idea, that the changes are adiabatic, so compression raises the temperature, and the correct result followed: the speed of sound depends only on the gas temperature and not on the pressure or the density.
Going further
Slide a slightly larger straw onto the end and use it like a trombone. Speed equals wavelength times frequency: at about 350 metres per second, a 350-hertz note has a wavelength of one metre.
tiles.src: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. I, ch. 47 · Exploratorium Science Snacks: Straw Oboe, Organ Pipe

tiles.cap: A $99 e-reader 5.95 mm thin that magnets to the back of your phone. Catch: no Kindle app
tiles.nums: the weight of the Xteink X4 Pro, with a 4.3-inch, 219-ppi screen and an 1100 mAh battery
tiles.p1: TIME put the Xteink X4 Pro on its Best Inventions of 2026 list on 15 October: an e-reader small enough to pocket that can magnetically snap to the back of a smartphone, now with a touchscreen, adjustable warm-and-cool front lighting and a larger battery. Xteink’s spec page: 4.3-inch screen at 219 ppi, 1100 mAh battery, 72 g, 111 × 69 × 5.95 mm, a 16 GB microSD card in the box (expandable to 256 GB), Wi-Fi 2.4 GHz and Bluetooth. There is no ebook storefront; its unlocked firmware means you upload your own EPUBs.
tiles.p2: What reviewers found wrong: TechRadar’s James Rogerson, after a month, called the interface “ugly and clunky”; no Android means it can’t run the Kindle or Kobo apps, and it charges through what he calls a “slightly fiddly proprietary charger” (a pogo-pin port, per Xteink) rather than USB-C.
deep: The engineering choice

Rogerson’s guess for the proprietary charger: “presumably in an effort to keep this as small as possible”. Xteink’s own FAQ confirms a charging cable is not included in the box. The battery “seems long-lasting too”, he wrote; Xteink gives no hours figure, only 1100 mAh.
Pixels

219 pixels per inch on a 4.3-inch screen; look up the ppi of your phone and compare. The screen is a front-lit panel with adjustable brightness and warm/cool light, and page turns work by tap, swipe or physical buttons.
The magnets

Rogerson: the magnets “weren’t strong enough to securely attach it to my phone while in a case”, and it can shift around and come loose in a pocket. He still called it “a pleasure to read books on”, and “thin enough that it doesn’t stick out much beyond the camera bump” of his iPhone.
Who it is for

Formats are EPUB and TXT, with JPG and BMP images. Because many bought ebooks need their DRM removed first, and new firmware must be flashed to get the most out of it, Rogerson “can’t really recommend this to the average ebook reader”. Price: $99 on Xteink’s site, down from a listed $129, though it was showing as sold out this weekend.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026, 15 Oct 2026 (Eliza Thompson) · Xteink spec page · TechRadar, 29 Aug 2026 (James Rogerson)

tiles.cap: Phone torch, mirror: watch your pupil snap shut, then overshoot. Now light the other eye
tiles.nums: your pupil’s diameter runs from 1.5 mm in bright light to more than 8 mm in the dark, says the Exploratorium
tiles.p1: Stand at a mirror and find the pupil, the black hole in the centre of your iris. Shine a light toward that eye (a phone torch, briefly, is fine) and watch the pupil contract. Notice that it takes longer for your pupil to dilate than it does to contract, and that it sometimes overshoots its mark: it shrinks down too far, then reopens slightly. Now shine the light into the other eye only, and watch the first one change anyway.
tiles.p2: Test it: in a dimly lit room, open and close one eye while watching the pupil of the other eye in the mirror. It moves even though its own light has not changed.
deep: Why it is black

The pupil is an opening that lets light into your eye. Since most of the light entering your eye does not escape, your pupil appears black. In dim light it expands to allow more light in; in bright light, it contracts.
The wiring

Light detected by the retina is converted to nerve impulses that travel down the optic nerve. Some go to the muscles that control the size of the pupil: more light creates more impulses, causing the muscles to close the pupil. Part of the optic nerve from one eye crosses over and couples to the muscles that control the pupil size of the other eye, which is why one pupil changes when you shine the light into the other.
A reflex, not a decision

The Exploratorium’s Shrinking Spot snack names it: the photopupillary reflex, controlled in the midbrain. Like all reflexes, its reaction is automatic, and because the midbrain always sends its messages to both irises, it occurs in both eyes even if only one eye is suddenly exposed to a change in light.
Bigger

Put a magnifying glass flat on the mirror and look into its centre. Light reflecting from your eye passes through the lens twice, once on its way to the mirror and once on its way back, so the image of your eye is magnified twice.
tiles.src: Exploratorium Science Snacks: Pupil; Shrinking Spot

tiles.cap: A 14-year-old boiled 24 plants from her family’s farm. 13 of them killed some bacteria
tiles.nums: farm plants whose extracts killed some bacteria; none worked as well as current medicines
tiles.p1: Locklyn Ward, 14, lives on a farm in Oklahoma. One evening while she was helping feed the cows, she got curious about the plants growing in the field, so she set out to see if any of them could take down bacteria. She picked 24 plants, 12 of them native to her state, cut them into one-gram pieces and boiled each to extract chemicals from it, then tested those extracts against two types of bacteria: Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus epidermidis.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: overuse of current antibiotics is leading to more drug-resistant bacteria, so new solutions are much needed. Her method needs a pot, paper disks and patience.
deep: The disk test
The test involved paper disks soaked in either the plant extracts or current antibiotics. If chemicals from the farm plants had antibiotic powers, the bacteria around those paper disks would die.
The result
No farm-plant extract worked as well as current medicines. But 13 of the 24 plants did kill some bacteria, including seven native plants.
Where the idea came from

“Growing up, my grandmother often talked with me about how plants and herbs can be used for medicine and healing,” Locklyn says. “And as a citizen of the Cherokee Nation, I’ve always been interested in learning more about plants and their traditional and potential medicinal uses.”
What it earned
A finalist spot in the 2026 Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge, a programme run by Society for Science, which also publishes Science News Explores.

tiles.cap: Two astronauts spent 7 h 11 min outside the ISS fitting a solar array. Next one: Thursday
tiles.nums: the station’s power once all eight roll-out arrays are in, up from 160 kW: an increase of up to 30%
tiles.p1: NASA astronaut Anil Menon and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Joshua Kutryk concluded their spacewalk outside the International Space Station at 3:08 p.m. EDT on 29 October, which is 3:08 on Friday morning in Singapore. During the 7-hour, 11-minute spacewalk they installed and deployed an International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array (IROSA) on the station’s 2A electrical power channel, the seventh IROSA installed on the station. It was U.S. spacewalk 100, Menon’s fourth and Kutryk’s first, and the 285th spacewalk in support of station assembly, maintenance and upgrades.
tiles.p2: Why it matters to you: the eighth and final IROSA goes on the 3B power channel in a spacewalk planned for Thursday 5 November, with NASA’s live coverage beginning at 6:45 a.m. (US Eastern time, which by then has gone back to standard time: 7:45 pm in Singapore).
deep: Riding the arm

The photo on this tile is NASA’s: Menon rides the Canadarm2 robotic arm to begin the installation of the roll-out solar array on the station’s port-side truss structure, while orbiting 260 miles above Earth.
How the array got there
The final pair of roll-out arrays flew up in the SpaceX Dragon cargo ship that launched on NASA’s 35th commercial resupply mission at 6:33 a.m. EDT on 13 October.
The power arithmetic

NASA: together, the eight arrays will increase available power by up to 30%, boosting the station’s power generation capacity from 160 kilowatts to approximately 215 kilowatts. Check it yourself: 215 divided by 160 comes to a little more than 1.3, so NASA’s “up to 30%” is a rounded figure.
Get-ahead work
Menon and Kutryk also completed several get-ahead tasks to prepare for the 5 November spacewalk. Watching the second one live is a Thursday-evening plan.
tiles.src: NASA Space Station blog, 29 Oct 2026 (Mark A. Garcia) · NASA release, 13 Oct 2026

tiles.cap: One muon crosses your hand about every second. On paper, almost none should reach you
tiles.nums: a muon’s mean lifetime at rest: at nearly the speed of light, that is only about 660 metres of travel
tiles.p1: Cosmic rays from space collide with atoms 15 to 20 kilometres up in the atmosphere. The collisions create pions, which decay into muons. A muon has a measured mean lifetime of about 2.2 microseconds; even at the speed of light it would travel on average only about 660 metres before decaying. From 15 km up, the trip takes 50 microseconds, more than twenty lifetimes, so almost no muons should reach the ground. Yet they arrive at ground level at about one per square centimetre per minute.
tiles.p2: The explanation is Einstein’s: time ticks slowly for particles moving at speeds close to that of light. In MIT’s version of the sum, a muon at 0.998 times the speed of light has a time-stretch factor of 15, and about one muon travels through your hand every second.
deep: The factor

The stretch is the Lorentz factor, 1/√(1 − v²/c²). For a 20 GeV muon, the CERN page gets it from E = mc²: the muon’s rest mass is 106 MeV, so the factor is 20 GeV divided by 106 MeV, which is 189. Its lifetime, as we see it, becomes 189 × 2.2 microseconds, and a significant fraction of the muons made in the upper atmosphere reach the ground.
MIT’s version

Prof. Markus Klute’s MIT lecture on muons: the lifetime is about 2.2 microseconds, the muons are produced at close to the speed of light, 0.998 times it, the classical distance works out to about 660 metres, and the gamma factor is 15; the clock in the muon, as observed by us, ticks much, much slower than for a muon at rest.
Muons as X-rays

Physics World: as many as 10,000 muons rain down on each square metre every minute, and muons at shallow angles can travel as far as 300 km before hitting the ground. Because they pass through rock, detectors placed beside volcanoes such as Sakurajima in Japan image the magma conduits inside, a technique called muography.
Discovery

Victor Hess found cosmic rays on a balloon flight in 1912, measuring the rate of ionisation as he ascended to 5300 metres. The muon itself was identified in 1937. At rest, CERN notes, it decays after only 2.2 microseconds into an electron and two kinds of neutrinos.
tiles.src: CERN High School Teachers programme: cosmic ray muons and relativistic time dilation · MIT OpenCourseWare 8.20, Prof. Markus Klute · Physics World, 25 Jul 2023 (Michael Allen) · home.cern

tiles.cap: A camera with a printer inside: 16 seconds a print, 15-second films, a dial of ten decades
tiles.nums: the print head’s resolution: 1600 × 600 dots exposed onto instax mini film in about 16 seconds
tiles.p1: Fujifilm’s Instax Mini Evo Cinema, in TIME’s Best Inventions of 2026, is two machines in one 270 g body styled like a Super 8 film camera. The camera half is a 1/5-inch CMOS sensor of approximately 5 million pixels behind an f/2.0 lens equivalent to 28 mm, recording 1920 × 2560 stills and 15-second video clips at 24 frames per second (600 × 800 in standard mode; 1080 × 1440 in a high-quality mode that works only with the 2020 setting and records to microSD) to internal memory or a microSD card up to 256 GB. The printer half exposes the digital image onto chemical instax mini film at 1600 × 600 dots, 40 × 80 µm per dot, in about 16 seconds; a full charge is good for approximately 100 prints.
tiles.p2: What reviewers found wrong: TechRadar’s Timothy Coleman, after two weeks, called operation “pretty sluggish”, saw a loading wheel almost every time he recorded a video or switched eras, had the camera freeze once until the battery drained, and judged the video “lo-fi at just HD 720p”; his cons list reads sluggish operation, poor image quality, video clip length limitations, pricey. Tom’s Guide’s Nikita Achanta found the print lever finicky and the camera expensive: US$409 at Tom’s Guide, US$419 at TechRadar.
deep: Why the print looks like film

The print is a real photochemical picture: instead of light from a lens, the print head exposes the instax film from the digital file, at 1600 × 600 dots. The print is only 1600 × 600 dots, far fewer than the sensor’s 1920 × 2560.
The Gen Dial

Twist it before shooting to apply one of ten effects named for the decades 1930 to 2020, inspired by a century of film formats, each with a degree control. The 1.54-inch LCD has approximately 170,000 dots and is not touch-sensitive.
The numbers that limit it

Shutter 1/4 to 1/8000 second and ISO 100 to 1600, both automatic. Video bitrate is 2.5 Mbps in standard mode and 9.0 Mbps in high quality, and each clip stops at about 15 seconds; internal memory holds approximately 50 shots and 10 clips. Charging takes 2 to 3 hours over USB-C, which is for charging only.
The verdict split

Coleman: “Technically speaking, this is a poor camera”, yet it still won his heart. Achanta: “one of the best instant cameras you can buy right now, period.” Both call it expensive; Achanta still lists its image and print quality as a plus.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 (Kevin Cortez) · Fujifilm specifications page · TechRadar (Timothy Coleman, updated 17 Feb 2026) · Tom’s Guide (Nikita Achanta, 4 Feb 2026)

tiles.p1: Behavioural scientist Benjamin Lira Luttges at Penn put it in six words. Hand the boring, repetitive stuff to the machine. Keep for yourself anything you want to become good at, and anything you enjoy. His colleague Trent Cash at Waterloo adds the mechanism: if we offload a specific skill to AI, we are probably not going to retain that skill particularly well.
tiles.p2: Why it is not scary: Cash also says humans are resilient and AI will not turn our brains to mush. It is a choice, made daily.
deep: The doctors who forgot
Doctors used an AI tool for three months to spot growths during colonoscopies. When it was switched off, they found fewer than before. Three months was enough for the skill to fade.
The readers who gave up

People who worked through SAT reading questions with AI help were more likely to skip questions once the help was removed. The researchers called that particularly concerning, because sticking with a hard question is itself the skill.
Your list
Write down three skills you want to be yours at 20. Those never get outsourced. Everything else is fair game.
tiles.src: Science News Explores · Cash et al. 2026 · Lira Luttges et al. 2026
